scenes.tts: Gregor Mendel crossed pea plants with purple flowers and pea plants with white flowers. Every offspring had purple flowers. Then those purple plants fertilized themselves. White flowers came back, in about one plant in four. Why do you look like your parents, but not exactly? And how can we predict the odds?
scenes.visual: Parent swatches purple and white cross to an all-purple row; the row self-fertilizes and one white swatch returns; the white one is held with a question mark and the essential question appears.

White flowers came back, in about one plant in four. Why do you look like your parents, but not exactly? And how can we predict the odds?

scenes.tts: A gene is a section of DNA. An allele is one version of a gene. Pea plants have a flower color gene, with a purple allele and a white allele. For most genes, body cells carry two alleles, one from each parent. We write alleles as letters: capital P for purple, small p for white.

scenes.visual: Two parallel DNA bars with a labelled gene block; the block gives two allele versions P and p; a cell outline takes two alleles, one from each parent.
scenes.narration: A gene is a section of DNA. An allele is one version of a gene. Pea plants have a flower color gene, with a purple allele and a white allele. For most genes, body cells carry two alleles, one from each parent. We write alleles as letters: capital P for purple, small p for white.

scenes.tts: A dominant allele shows its trait even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive. The pair of alleles is the genotype. The trait you can see is the phenotype. Same two alleles: homozygous. Different alleles: heterozygous. So a plant with capital P and small p looks purple, but it still carries a white allele.

scenes.tts: When a heterozygous plant makes sex cells, its two alleles separate. Each sex cell gets one allele. Scientists call this the law of segregation. Probability is the chance that something will happen, from zero, never, to one, always. Each sex cell has a fifty percent chance of carrying capital P, and a fifty percent chance of carrying small p.

scenes.tts: A Punnett square is a grid. It shows every way one sex cell from each parent can combine. Put one parent's sex cells across the top, and the other parent's down the side. Cross two heterozygous plants. The boxes read capital P capital P, capital P small p, capital P small p, and small p small p. Each box has a one in four chance. Three boxes look purple. One looks white.

Cross two heterozygous plants. The boxes read PP, Pp, Pp, and pp. Each box has a 1 in 4 chance. Three boxes look purple. One looks white.

scenes.tts: So where was the white hiding? Inside each heterozygous plant, as a white allele. Each offspring had a one in four chance of getting two white alleles, and about one plant in four did. But a Punnett square gives chances, not certainties. Four seeds from two heterozygous plants could include no white plants at all.
